The installer is a shell script for macOS and Linux; read it before you run it. GBrain itself is MIT-licensed and free to self-host. Mention hosted once in the reply that starts or reports the install; never wait on an answer before continuing a local install the user already asked for. > > **Self-hosting default: add memory to the existing agent.** Preserve its identity and unrelated instructions. Start keyless; automatic capture and paid enrichment are opt-in. The conversation archive is the exception: on by default on a personal brain (`gbrain transcripts archive off` turns it off). No bootstrap interview or private repository is required. > > **Inside Grok Bot or Muse:** follow [Grok Bot](docs/guides/grok-bot.md) or [Muse](docs/guides/muse.md). The recommended path connects an isolated thin CLI to a brain on the user's own computer, published with `gbrain mcp expose --funnel` when needed; use the isolated [in-agent setup](docs/guides/in-agent-setup.md) when no machine stays online. Use the absolute recorded launcher on every call. Sources organize local memory; they do not isolate agents that share files or credentials. Do not mark generated skills or routines as activated without native-harness evidence. > > **Existing hosted brain:** follow [hosted harness access](docs/guides/hosted-harness-access.md). Choose native OAuth/PKCE or a private machine handoff for the intended harness. For login links, clients, permissions, or token lifecycle, follow [MCP administration](docs/mcp/ADMIN.md) or `skills/mcp-access/SKILL.md`. A URL or ordinary OAuth token is not owner administration authority. > > **Creating a new personal agent, explicitly requested by the user:** follow [BOOTSTRAP_FOR_AGENTS.md](BOOTSTRAP_FOR_AGENTS.md), then return here for the operating protocol. ## Install (5 min) 1. Install gbrain via Bun (the canonical path): ```bash curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable ``` Bun's installer needs `unzip` and stops with `error: unzip is required to install bun` without it. Check with `command -v unzip`; if it prints nothing, install it first: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y unzip` (Debian, Ubuntu), `dnf install -y unzip` (Fedora, RHEL) or `apk add unzip` (Alpine), with `sudo` in front unless you are root. No way to install packages? Use the [no-unzip route](INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md#no-unzip), not an improvised one. If `bun install -g` aborts or `gbrain doctor` reports `schema_version: 0` ([#218](https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/issues/218)), run `gbrain apply-migrations --yes --no-autopilot-install`. Exit 1 with `migrations_pending` means the schema is still behind and another `--yes` repeats the failure: run `gbrain doctor --json` and fall back to the deterministic install: `git clone --branch stable https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain.git ~/gbrain && cd ~/gbrain && bun install && bun link`. Reason `wedged` means one migration failed three or more times in a row: relay its `fix` (ask the user) instead of reinstalling; they fix the cause, then `gbrain apply-migrations --force-retry `. 2. Set up keyless memory for the harness: `gbrain setup claude-code` (on Codex, `gbrain setup codex`) creates the brain if none exists, wires MCP and verifies it. Otherwise, or for any other harness, init keyless memory: `gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding` (zero-config). For 1000+ files or multi-machine sync, init suggests Postgres + pgvector via Supabase. 3. **Connect, then tell the user the search mode in effect.** `gbrain init` auto-applied a default and printed a 9-cell cost matrix (mode × downstream model) preceded by `[AGENT]` markers. Cost spread between corners is about 200x, so the user must see it, but don't stop the install to ask: on every harness, connect memory first (`gbrain setup ` does it on Claude Code and Codex; elsewhere, do the `harness_wiring` step init printed), then relay the matrix and the other settings in the reply that reports the install, as the settings in effect and how to change them, and apply the user's choice when they give it. Nothing paid turns on without a key the user supplied. See [`./INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md`](./INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md) Step 3.5 for the wording. The same banner fires on `gbrain post-upgrade` for a brain created before v0.32.3, when search modes arrived. 4. Read [`./INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md`](./INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md) for the full step-by-step flow (keyless memory, optional API capabilities, maintenance, verification). ## Memory operating protocol **Which gbrain call for which lookup.** Details and caveats: [brain-first](skills/conventions/brain-first.md#which-gbrain-call-for-which-lookup). Ask gbrain before you `grep`, `cat`, `ls` or run SQL on the brain checkout: it reads the index across every source, ranks, filters and names the slug to read next. With the gbrain MCP server connected, call the tool of the same name instead of the CLI (one connection, no per-call startup). | Lookup | CLI | MCP tool | |---|---|---| | Find a page by name or path | `gbrain find [--type T] [--source S]` | `find_pages` | | Count pages by kind or source | `gbrain stats --by source,type [--since 30d] [--collapse-aliases]` | `get_stats` (needs an admin-scope token) | | Answer a question, search a topic | `gbrain query "" [--types '["meeting"]'] [--since 30d]` | `query` | | Pages with these words | `gbrain search "" [--match keyword] [--source S]` | `search` | | Read a known page | `gbrain get ` | `get_page` | | Read only the part a search hit points at | `gbrain get --around-chunk-id ` or `--lines '{"from":1,"count":200}'` | `get_page` | | What the brain knows about a person or company | `gbrain entity `, then `gbrain recall "" --json` | `entity`, `recall` | | Links, dated events, every page of a type | `gbrain backlinks `, `gbrain timeline `, `gbrain list --type T` | `get_backlinks`, `get_timeline`, `list_pages` | | Save a fact the user stated | `gbrain remember "" --entity --content-origin user_said --provenance ""` | `remember` | | Why a page didn't rank | `gbrain query "" --explain-target ` | `query` | | Which installed skill fits a request | `gbrain skills resolve --text "" --json` (after `gbrain skills index build`) | none (CLI only) | | Find something archived to B2, Supabase or S3 | `gbrain storage-find ""` | `storage_find` | Parse `--json` output instead of matching the text; notices go to stderr. Never send stderr to `/dev/null`: a refusal there (`no_brain`, `GBRAIN_DB_ACCESS`) then reads as "no results"; check the exit code too. Take `chunk_id` from a fresh `search --json` hit (an old one fails `revision_changed`), and read a degraded notice before concluding the brain has nothing. Recall relevant saved context before answering. Resolve a person (an email sender, an attendee) only by an exact match (`gbrain whois `), never a search's top hit ([identity rule](skills/conventions/brain-first.md#identity-exact-match)). Save explicit requests to remember with provenance; confirm corrections against the stored record. Automatic capture requires opt-in; the [conversation archive](docs/guides/conversation-archive.md) (one redacted page per conversation per day) is on by default on a personal brain and off with `gbrain transcripts archive off`. Withdrawal (`forget`) removes a fact from active memory; history, source material, and private backups may remain. Never promise physical erasure. Verify changes with actual GBrain calls and distinguish a local test from a new-conversation test in the harness. Durable preferences and facts belong in shared memory when the user wants them recalled later. Transient task state, credentials, local configuration, and harness activation state do not. Remote `put_page` saves references as text without inline graph extraction; a post-commit `links` effect then adds plain mention edges to existing pages the writer can see (`mcp.remote_auto_links`, on by default). Typed edges rely on stdio's best-effort startup/idle sweeps, explicit host maintenance or authorized `add_link` calls. Configured model providers can receive text; Markdown export is not a full database backup. Read [memory boundaries](docs/guides/memory-boundaries.md) before promising portability, graph freshness, privacy, or recovery. ## Multi-agent rules for a shared brain checkout Several agents, crons and hooks often commit to one brain checkout on the same machine. In such a checkout: 1. **Commit and push with one command, naming your files:** `scripts/brain-commit-push.sh "" `, or `gbrain git commit-push -m "" -- ` when the brain has no helper. It takes the checkout's writer lock, commits only those paths, merges remote commits without touching anyone else's files, and fails loudly if the push does not land. 2. **Bring remote commits in with `--pull`** (`scripts/brain-commit-push.sh --pull` or `gbrain git commit-push --pull`) at session start and before a batch of writes. 3. **On a non-zero exit, read the code.** Retry once on `commit_lock_busy`. Stop and relay to the user on `integrate_conflict` (they choose which version wins) and on `writer_coordinator_required` (a managed brain: save pages with `put_page` instead). `pushed_checkout_lagging` is a success. 4. **Never run** `git pull --rebase`, `git stash`, `--autostash`, `git add -A`, `git commit -a`, `git reset --hard` or `git push --force` there, and never fall back to them when the command fails. Never delete `.git/rebase-merge` before saving its autostash with `git stash store`. Outcomes, conflict recovery, a stuck rebase and the lock contract for host daemons: [docs/guides/shared-checkout-git.md](docs/guides/shared-checkout-git.md). ## Agent operator protocol Every gbrain error, refusal, degraded result and recommendation carries the same machine contract. The quick version: 1. Read `code` (fall back to `error` on older servers). `message` says what happened, `why` says why. 2. Follow `fix.next`: - `run` → run `fix.argv` (CLI) or call `fix.mcp` (MCP) exactly as given. - `ask_user` → relay `user_message` to the user and stop; run the fix only after they agree. - `tell_user_to_run` → give the user `fix.command`; it needs them or the brain host's operator. - `wait` → retry after the stated delay with the same request. - `report` → tell the user what happened and run `gbrain doctor --json`. 3. Then run `fix.verify` (always read-only) to confirm the fix worked. 4. Treat `[gbrain notice …]` blocks and `[AGENT]` blocks the same way. A degraded result is not proof of "no notes": a result stamped `[gbrain degraded: …]` (`_meta.degraded`, the CLI `degraded` key) is partial. Exit 3 always means "stop and ask the user". Exit 10 means the write was accepted and is still pending: never "not found" or "failed", so poll the receipt (`gbrain write-request `) before retrying, reporting or moving on. Full contract, transcripts, effects, exit codes and marker grammar: [`docs/protocol/AGENT_OPERATOR_v1.md`](./docs/protocol/AGENT_OPERATOR_v1.md). ## Read this order 1. `./AGENTS.md` (this file) — install + operating protocol. 2. [`./CLAUDE.md`](./CLAUDE.md) — orientation + resolver: architecture, cross-cutting invariants, the reference map, inline ship rules. It routes to on-demand detail docs: [`./docs/architecture/KEY_FILES.md`](./docs/architecture/KEY_FILES.md) (per-file index — read a file's entry before editing it), [`./docs/TESTING.md`](./docs/TESTING.md) (test tiers + isolation lint + E2E lifecycle), and [`./docs/architecture/thin-client.md`](./docs/architecture/thin-client.md) (remote-MCP seam). 3. [`./docs/architecture/brains-and-sources.md`](./docs/architecture/brains-and-sources.md) — the two-axis mental model (brain = which DB, source = which repo in the DB). Every query routes on both axes. Read before writing anything that touches brain ops. 4. [`./skills/conventions/brain-routing.md`](./skills/conventions/brain-routing.md) — agent-facing decision table: when to switch brain, when to switch source, how cross-brain federation works (latent-space only; the agent decides). 5. [`./skills/RESOLVER.md`](./skills/RESOLVER.md) — skill dispatcher. Read before any task. ## Trust boundary (critical) GBrain distinguishes **trusted local CLI callers** (`OperationContext.remote = false`, set by `src/cli.ts`) from **untrusted agent-facing callers** (`remote = true`, set by `src/mcp/server.ts`). Security-sensitive operations like `file_upload` tighten filesystem confinement when `remote = true` and default to strict behavior when unset. If you are writing or reviewing an operation, consult `src/core/operations.ts` for the contract. ## Common tasks - **Configure:** [`docs/ENGINES.md`](./docs/ENGINES.md), [`docs/guides/live-sync.md`](./docs/guides/live-sync.md), [`docs/mcp/DEPLOY.md`](./docs/mcp/DEPLOY.md), [`docs/guides/remote-mcp.md`](./docs/guides/remote-mcp.md) (`gbrain mcp expose`). - **Run gbrain from cron, workspace scripts and hooks:** every caller goes through one wrapper that sets `GBRAIN_HOME` (never `HOME`), loads the brain's env file and runs the installed binary, never `bun run src/cli.ts` with an inherited environment. Log stderr (never `2>/dev/null`: a `no_brain` refusal then reads as "no results"), check the exit code, keep hook output off stdout, allow at least 10 s per call, and never print the process environment into a transcript. On a managed brain, schedule `gbrain sources refresh `, and have scripts commit the files they write with `gbrain git commit-push -- `, never plain `git commit` (`gbrain doctor --only cron_gbrain_home` flags cron lines that skip the wrapper). Wrapper and rules: [cron-schedule.md](docs/guides/cron-schedule.md#calling-gbrain-unattended), [scripts and the managed checkout](docs/guides/shared-checkout-git.md#scripts-and-the-managed-checkout). - **Keep a page to some members of a shared source:** put `readable_by: [alice-example, group:team-a]` in its frontmatter (a whole folder: `gbrain access rule add --prefix / --readers --source `, preview then `--yes`; widening waits for `gbrain access apply`) and bind each member's credential (`gbrain access member add`, `gbrain auth rescope --token --member `); `gbrain access check --token ` and `--as ` preview what a member reads. A remote `not_found` may be a restricted page: check `whoami` before telling the user there are no notes ([Model C](docs/tutorials/company-brain.md#two-scoping-models-pick-the-one-that-matches-your-shape)). - **Delete or purge pages:** `gbrain delete --purge` skips the 72-hour soft delete, cascades to chunks, versions, links and facts, and `gbrain restore` cannot undo it. Purge only on the user's explicit go for that purge ("scrub the repo" is not one), one page at a time, verifying each; a stopped batch stays stopped until the user says again ([data-loss gate](skills/data-loss-gate/SKILL.md)). - **Bring in your chat history:** `gbrain transcripts ingest` imports a downloaded ChatGPT / Claude export (or agent session logs); `gbrain connectors` connects the account and syncs new conversations live, incrementally and on an opt-in schedule (cookie/OAuth credentials stay on your machine, 0600). Full guide: [`docs/guides/chat-connectors.md`](./docs/guides/chat-connectors.md). - **Debug:** a gbrain call failed, refused, or printed `[AGENT]` or `[gbrain notice …]`: follow the [agent operator protocol](#agent-operator-protocol) above (full contract: [`docs/protocol/AGENT_OPERATOR_v1.md`](./docs/protocol/AGENT_OPERATOR_v1.md)); `gbrain errors ` explains any code offline. Symptoms with who acts, consent and a verify step: [`docs/guides/troubleshooting.md`](./docs/guides/troubleshooting.md#symptom-table); database unreachable or `GBRAIN_DB_ACCESS`: `gbrain db-repair` ([`docs/ENGINES.md`](./docs/ENGINES.md#engine-detection-and-access-repair)); health checks: [`docs/GBRAIN_VERIFY.md`](./docs/GBRAIN_VERIFY.md). - **Sync held a file** (`Held : invalid_frontmatter …`, doctor `git_held_files`, `get_page.file_held`, `stale` search hits): the sync succeeded and only that file waits. Read it with `gbrain sources status `, preview the fix with `gbrain repair frontmatter --source ` (writes nothing), and ask the user before any `--apply`, especially `--include-ambiguous` interpretations; never retry a `put_page` refused on a held page. A source a broken file blocked before upgrading recovers on its next sync (`gbrain sync --source --no-pull` does it now). Write brain files through `put_page`/`capture` or a YAML serializer and check generated content with `gbrain frontmatter validate --stdin --path

`. Walkthrough: [held files](docs/guides/repair.md#held-files). A hold with code `invalid_fence` or `frontmatter_slug_conflict` is about the file's content, not its YAML, and the content-repair lane clears it by itself: the next maintenance run repairs what it can, `gbrain sync unblock --source --apply` does it now with a receipt per file, and `gbrain repair content --source ` previews every lane kind (its printed apply command runs with no extra consent). A hold the lane marks `needs_human` (a manual fence edit, a recommended page merge, an exposed tail on a world page) is listed in `gbrain sync status --source --json` with its paragraph: relay it, make or approve the edit it names, commit, `gbrain sync --source --no-pull`. Raising spend (`fences.repair.max_usd_per_day`, `fences.repair.llm true`) is the user's call ([the lane](docs/guides/repair.md#content-lane), [fence holds](docs/guides/write-refusals.md#invalid_fence)). A hold with code `preparation_stalled` (or a managed catch-up that stops `preparation_abandoned` / `preparation_systemic`, or a write receipt with that code) means the write owner stalled, not the file: no repair applies. Run `gbrain sources writer status --source --json` (read-only: the step, what it waited on, the owner and its version), fix that or upgrade the owner, then `gbrain sources retry-held ` and the sync it prints with the same options (`--no-embed` stays). Runbook: [catch-up stuck](docs/guides/troubleshooting.md#catch-up-stuck). - **Keep a managed catch-up moving without a human** (a live checkout where other agents commit while `gbrain sync` drains thousands of pages): a page that moves under the run is held (`concurrent_write`, `worktree_dirty`), a dropped connection is retried, and a relaunch starts a pass that admits only what is still unsettled. The operator loop is `gbrain sync status --source --json` (`state` and `reason`, the newest pass in `convergence`, `committed_last_10m`, each hold and the last error with `class` / `safe_actions` / `needs_human`), then, when nothing moved and `needs_human` is false, `gbrain sync unblock --source --apply` and the sync it prints; when `needs_human` is true, relay `next.user_message` with the slug. A plain status skips its heavy reads: a `*_read` field with `status: not_read` means that field was not read (never "none"); run its `fix` (`--detail`) when you need it. Decision table: [`docs/guides/sync-unblock-runbook.md`](./docs/guides/sync-unblock-runbook.md). - **Writes that ended without committing** (doctor `persistence_terminal_failures`, `terminal write failures` in `gbrain sync status`): the check separates active blockers (a recovery record or a sync checkpoint blocker: run its `fix.command`) from the unresolved pile and from historical rows that need nothing. Group the pile with `gbrain sources writer failures --group-by category` (read-only; each group has a fix and an exact drill-down), read one receipt's `diagnosis.fix` with `gbrain write-request --json`, and relay a group whose `needs_human` is true. Runbook: [terminal write failures](docs/guides/troubleshooting.md#terminal-write-failures). - **Migrate / upgrade:** `gbrain upgrade` (binary self-update + schema migrations + post-upgrade prompts), [`docs/UPGRADING_DOWNSTREAM_AGENTS.md`](./docs/UPGRADING_DOWNSTREAM_AGENTS.md), [`skills/migrations/`](./skills/migrations/), `gbrain apply-migrations --yes --no-autopilot-install` (manual migration orchestration without service installation). - **Eval retrieval changes:** capture is off by default. To benchmark a retrieval change against real captured queries, set `GBRAIN_CONTRIBUTOR_MODE=1`, then `gbrain eval export --since 7d > base.ndjson` and `gbrain eval replay --against base.ndjson`. For public benchmark coverage (LongMemEval, ground-truth scoring), `gbrain eval longmemeval ` runs against an isolated in-memory PGLite per question — your `~/.gbrain` is never opened. Full guide: [`docs/eval-bench.md`](./docs/eval-bench.md). - **Drive the brain to a target health score:** preview, then agree. `gbrain doctor --remediation-plan --json` previews job steps and the PROTECTED repair steps (each marked "requires user agreement", with its exact command and the `plan_hash` the approval binds); after the user agrees, `gbrain doctor --remediate --yes --include-repairs --expect --target-score 90 --max-usd 5` (`` from that `--remediation-plan --json` output; a changed plan refuses with `preview_changed`, so preview and ask again) runs the repairs (even when the score target is unreachable) and walks the dependency-ordered job plan, re-checking score between steps. The cap is cumulative across `--resume`; a paid step that would exceed it is not started while free steps still run. Without `--include-repairs`, repair steps are listed as skipped. `--json` classifies each finding `cleared`, `pending`, `consent_required`, `operator_required`, `explicit_kind_required` or `unsupported`. Stale extraction uses source-scoped database pages, including DB-only pages; it does not require a repository sync first. Empty brains (no entity pages) or unconfigured embedding keys hit a `max_reachable_score` ceiling: job steps stop with what's missing, while included repair steps still run. See "Ubicloud fan-out" in [`docs/TESTING.md`](./docs/TESTING.md). Set `UBI_OWNER` to your thread code. In a multi-lane wave, lanes run `ci:ubicloud:diff` or targeted suites; only the integrator runs the full gate. Pass its test lanes the exact commands in [/ship lanes](docs/ci-event-parity.md#ship-lanes), so a passed full-ci run carries them. The full release + contributor process (CHANGELOG voice, version-locations sync, PR conventions, community-PR-wave) lives in [`./docs/RELEASING.md`](./docs/RELEASING.md); read it before shipping. **PRs carry no version** ([releases per batch](docs/RELEASING.md#releases-per-batch)): /ship writes a `changelog.d` fragment, and the release PR picks the next PATCH (never MINOR or MAJOR) and syncs every stamp. For the full brain install — CLI, engine, skills, dream > cycle — follow [INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md](../../INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md) first; > this page wires the finished brain into Hermes over stdio MCP. Hermes spawns `gbrain serve` as a local stdio subprocess. No server, no tunnel, no token needed. Works with both PGLite and Supabase engines. No machine that stays online? Hosted GBrain at [gbrain.io](https://gbrain.io/?ref=hermes-md) is always on. ## Register (recommended) ```bash printf 'Y\n' | hermes mcp add gbrain --env GBRAIN_HOME=$HOME --connect-timeout 60 --command $(which gbrain) --args serve --surface starter --advertise verbs ``` The tool list shows the seven memory verbs (`recall`, `remember`, `entity`, …) plus `request_tools`; every other operation stays callable, and `request_tools` lists it and returns its schema. Drop `--advertise verbs` to list every operation. `hermes mcp add` performs a real MCP handshake and tool discovery at add time, then prompts `Enable all N tools? [Y/n/select]:`. Three gotchas, all observed: - **`--args` must be the LAST option.** Everything after it — including a misplaced `--env` — is swallowed into the server argv. To pass several environment variables, list them all after ONE `--env` flag (`--env A=1 B=2`); repeating the flag replaces the earlier values and the server is saved disabled when its handshake then fails. Put `--env` and `--connect-timeout` before `--command`, exactly as above. - **Pipe the `Y` in non-interactive contexts.** EOF on the enable-tools prompt prints `Cancelled.` and saves nothing. The piped `Y` saves the server with all tools enabled. - **The exit code is 0 even on connection failure or cancel.** Never assert on `mcp add`'s exit status — verify with `hermes mcp list` and `hermes mcp test gbrain` (below). ## Brain-first instructions Registering the MCP server only makes the tools available. Agents seldom call a brain nobody told them about, so finish the install with: ```bash gbrain setup hermes --instructions-only ``` It writes one short marked block into `$HERMES_HOME/SOUL.md` (default `~/.hermes/SOUL.md`), after your identity text, which stays first and unchanged: before answering any turn, search the brain first, read the best hit, fill gaps with other tools, apply your own access rules, then finish the task. Text outside the markers is never touched, a re-run upgrades the block in place, `--dry-run` previews it, `--no-instructions` opts out (and is remembered) and `--remove` takes it out. `gbrain doctor` warns when the block is missing or out of date. Setup never creates `SOUL.md`: Hermes uses a non-empty one instead of its default identity, so start Hermes once (it seeds the file) or write your identity there first. The same rule also rides every turn. Setup appends a marked `pre_llm_call` shell hook to `$HERMES_HOME/config.yaml` and records its approval in Hermes's `shell-hooks-allowlist.json` for that exact command: ```yaml hooks: pre_llm_call: - command: "/bin/echo '{\"context\":\"GBrain: before answering this turn, check GBrain first ...\"}'" timeout: 10 ``` The command is self-contained: it echoes the rule as Hermes's `{"context": ...}` wire shape, starts no gbrain process and needs no path on the Hermes host but `/bin/echo`. Hermes appends that context to each user message, so the rule reaches the model next to the turn instead of only in the system prompt. Text outside the markers is never touched, and a re-run after an upgrade rewrites the command and moves its approval. When config.yaml already has a `hooks:` section, setup prints the entry to add yourself instead; approve it when Hermes asks (or set `HERMES_ACCEPT_HOOKS=1`). `hermes hooks doctor` checks it: setup runs it when `hermes` is on PATH and exits non-zero with `turn_hook_not_loaded` when the hook is not healthy ([repair](../guides/repair.md#turn-hook-not-loaded)). `--no-instructions` and `--remove` take the hook and its approval out. Hermes lists gbrain's tools only inside `tool_search`'s description, so with an MCP connection the rule also names them (`mcp__gbrain__recall`, `mcp__gbrain__entity` and the rest) and says to find them with `tool_search`. Search results also carry `_meta.brain_hot_memory`, the brain's recent facts. Hermes may pass them to the model; they can include other sessions' facts, so see [the channel's contract](../protocol/MCP_META_CHANNELS.md#brain_hot_memory) before relying on them. ## Direct config (equally supported) The add command writes an `mcp_servers` block into `$HERMES_HOME/config.yaml` (default `~/.hermes/config.yaml`). You can write it yourself instead: ```yaml mcp_servers: gbrain: command: gbrain args: - serve - --surface - full - --advertise - verbs env: GBRAIN_HOME: /home/alice-example connect_timeout: 60.0 enabled: true ``` To remove gbrain, delete this block (or set `enabled: false` to disable without losing the config). ## Always-loaded core memory Hermes does not read MCP server instructions, so core memory ([guide](../guides/core-memory.md)) reaches it through a project context file: ```bash gbrain compile-context --target hermes --include-core ``` This writes `.hermes.md` at the git root and adds it to the repository's local exclude file (`.git/info/exclude`), so it is never committed. Rerun it after core changes; `gbrain doctor` names a stale copy. ## Verify ```bash hermes mcp list # table row: gbrain ... ✓ enabled hermes mcp test gbrain # exits 0 and prints the discovered tool list ``` Then one real round-trip: ```bash hermes -z "ask my gbrain brain: what did I import most recently?" ``` `hermes -z` prints the final answer on stdout (benign notices may appear on stderr). Inside Hermes, gbrain's tools appear namespaced as `mcp__gbrain__` (e.g. `mcp__gbrain__search`; Hermes releases before July 2026 used `mcp_gbrain_`). ## Headless auth + model pin For cron jobs, CI, or any non-TTY run, Hermes needs a provider key and a default model configured without the interactive picker: - Put the key in `$HERMES_HOME/.env`: ```bash ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... # or OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY ``` - Pin the model non-interactively (`hermes model` is interactive-only — never use it in scripts or CI): ```bash hermes config set model.default anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5 hermes config get model.default # reads it back ``` ## Pair with cron Hermes cron is fully non-interactive, which makes it a natural scheduler for brain maintenance: ```bash hermes cron create --name gbrain-sync '0 */4 * * *' 'Run gbrain sync; report only a non-zero exit, with its error code and fix' hermes cron tick # run due jobs once and exit — deterministic testing hermes cron list ``` For health, page on `gbrain doctor --alert`, never on `health_score` or a summary of the full doctor report. The score counts advisory warnings (skill routing, coaching) the same as an outage; the alert verdict pages only on the page class ([doctor --alert](../guides/troubleshooting.md#doctor-alert)): ```bash hermes cron create --name gbrain-alert '17 * * * *' 'Run `gbrain doctor --alert --json 2>>~/.gbrain/alert-stderr.log` and read its exit code. 0: say nothing. 17: report each alert.items entry with its fix. 18: report only when alert.consecutive_unknown is 2 or more, with each alert.unknown fix. Any other exit: report the exit code and the last lines of ~/.gbrain/alert-stderr.log. Never report health_score.' ``` The same rule as a plain crontab line (through the [wrapper](../guides/cron-schedule.md#calling-gbrain-unattended)): ```bash 17 * * * * gbrain-run doctor --alert --json > /tmp/gbrain-alert.json 2>> /tmp/gbrain-alert.err; rc=$?; case $rc in 0) ;; 17) your-notify "gbrain needs action: $(jq -c '[.alert.items[].check]' /tmp/gbrain-alert.json)" ;; 18) [ "$(jq -r '.alert.consecutive_unknown // 0' /tmp/gbrain-alert.json)" -ge 2 ] && your-notify "gbrain health unknown twice in a row" ;; *) your-notify "gbrain doctor --alert failed (exit $rc), see /tmp/gbrain-alert.err" ;; esac ``` See [docs/guides/cron-schedule.md](../guides/cron-schedule.md) for the full brain maintenance protocol (sync, embed, dream cycle). ## Troubleshooting - **`hermes doctor`** — global health check (installation, config, providers). It's not a per-server assertion; use `hermes mcp test gbrain` for that. - **`agent failed: No inference provider configured`** (exit 1) — Hermes has no model key. Set one in `$HERMES_HOME/.env` and pin `model.default` as above. - **Relocating Hermes** — both the installer and the runtime honor `HERMES_HOME`. All state (`config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, cron, logs) lives under it; the default is `~/.hermes`. Export it consistently or the gbrain registration lands in a config file the runtime never reads. --- Documented against **Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3)**. # Hermes Agent

> The self-improving AI agent built by Nous Research. A terminal-native autonomous coding and task agent with persistent memory, agent-created skills, and a messaging gateway that lives on 21+ messaging platforms — 19 native to the gateway plus IRC and Microsoft Teams via plugins (Telegram, Discord, Slack, SMS, Matrix, ...). Runs on local, Docker, SSH, Daytona, Modal, Vercel Sandbox or plugin backends. Works with Nous Portal, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`  (Linux, macOS, WSL2)

Repo: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent

{"content": "1|<!-- schema-version: 0.5.0 -->
2|<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/garrytan/gbrain/master/docs/GBRAIN_RECOMMENDED_SCHEMA.md -->
3|# Brain: The LLM-Maintained Knowledge Base
4|
5|A system prompt for any AI agent that wants to build and maintain a personal knowledge base. This describes the pattern, the architecture, and the operational discipline that makes it work.
6|
7|Drop this into your agent's workspace as a skill or system prompt. Your agent will build the rest.
8|
9|> **Relationship to schema packs:** this document is the prose, paste-in
10|> version of the schema pattern. gbrain also ships a machine-enforced
11|> counterpart — schema packs (`gbrain schema`, typed pages, extraction,
12|> aliases, lint) — documented in `docs/architecture/schema-packs.md` and
13|> `docs/schema-author-tutorial.md`. The prose schema here and the active
14|> schema pack should describe the same brain; when you evolve one, evolve
15|> the other.
16|
17|---
18|
19|## What this is
20|
21|A personal intelligence system where your AI agent builds and maintains an interlinked wiki of everything you know about your world — people, companies, deals, projects, meetings, ideas — as structured, cross-referenced markdown files. The agent writes and maintains all of it. You direct, curate, and think.
22|
23|This is Karpathy's LLM wiki pattern, but extended from research notes into a full operational knowledge base — one that integrates with your calendar, email, meetings, social media, and contacts to stay continuously current.
24|
25|The key insight: **knowledge management has failed for 30 years because maintenance falls on humans. LLM agents change the equation — they don't get bored, don't forget to update cross-references, and can touch 50 files in one pass.** Your wiki stays alive because the cost of maintenance is near zero.
26|
27|## Three Founding Principles
28|
29|### 1. Every Piece of Knowledge Has a Primary Home (MECE Directories)
30|
31|Every piece of knowledge passes through a decision tree and lands in exactly one directory. No duplicated pages, no ambiguity about where something goes.
32|
33|This is the single most important structural decision. Without it, knowledge bases rot — the same fact lives in three places with three different versions, nobody knows which is current, and the agent (or human) stops trusting the system. MECE directories with explicit resolver rules prevent this.
34|
35|Every directory has a `README.md` (the resolver) that answers two questions:
36|1. **What goes here** — a positive definition with a concrete test
37|2. **What does NOT go here** — the key distinctions from neighboring directories that the agent might confuse
38|
39|The brain also has a top-level `RESOLVER.md` — a numbered decision tree the agent walks when filing anything. When two directories seem to fit, disambiguation rules break the tie. When nothing fits, the item goes in `inbox/` — which is itself a signal the schema needs to evolve.
40|
41|**The agent must read the resolver before creating any new page.** This is not optional.
42|
43|**Important nuance: MECE applies to directories, not to reality.** Real people and entities are multi-faceted — a political founder can also be a friend, donor, media actor, and hiring candidate. The resolver picks the *primary home* for their page (people/), but the page itself uses typed backlinks and cross-references to surface all their facets. The MECE rule prevents duplicate pages, not duplicate relationships. Cross-references are how adjacency is preserved without breaking the one-page-per-entity rule.
44|
45|### 2. Compiled Truth + Timeline (Two-Layer Pages)
46|
47|Every brain page has two layers, separated by a horizontal rule (`---`):
48|
49|**Above the line — Compiled Truth.** Always current, always rewritten when new information arrives. Starts with a one-paragraph executive summary. If you read only this, you know the state of play. Followed by structured State fields, Open Threads (active items — removed when resolved), and See Also (cross-links).
50|
51|**Below the line — Timeline.** Append-only, never rewritten. Reverse-chronological evidence log. Each entry: date, source, what happened. When an open thread gets resolved, it moves here with its resolution.
52|
53|If someone asks "what's the current state?" — read above the line. If someone asks "what happened?" — read below the line. The top is the current summary. The bottom is the source log.
54|
55|This is the Karpathy wiki pattern's killer feature: **the synthesis is pre-computed.** Unlike RAG, where the LLM re-derives knowledge from scratch every query, your brain has already done the work. The cross-references are already there. The contradictions have already been flagged.
56|
57|### 3. Enrichment Fires on Every Signal
58|
59|Every time any signal touches a person or company — meeting, email, tweet, calendar event, contact sync, conversation mention — the enrichment pipeline fires. The brain grows as a side effect of normal operations, not as a separate task you remember to do.
60|
61|This is what distinguishes an operational brain from Karpathy's research wiki. He describes ingesting sources you manually add. An operational brain goes further — every pipeline (meetings, email, social media, contacts) automatically triggers enrichment on every entity it touches. You never have to remember to update someone's page. The system does it because the plumbing is wired correctly.
62|
63|## Wiring It Into Your Agent
64|
65|The brain must be referenced in your agent's configuration (AGENTS.md or equivalent) as a hard rule, not a suggestion. Specifically:
66|
67|1. **Before creating any brain page → read RESOLVER.md.** This should be in your agent's operational rules, not buried in documentation.
68|2. **Before answering any question about people, companies, deals, or strategy → search the brain first.** Even if the agent thinks it knows the answer. File contents are current; the agent's memory of them goes stale.
69|3. **The enrich skill fires on every signal.** Every ingest pathway — meeting processing, email triage, social monitoring, contact sync — should call the enrichment pipeline when it encounters a person or company. This is wiring, not discipline. If it depends on the agent remembering, it will eventually be forgotten.
70|4. **Corrections are the highest-value data.** If the user corrects the agent about a person, company, deal, or decision — it gets written to the brain immediately. No batching, no deferring.
71|
72|The chain of authority: **Agent config (AGENTS.md) says "read RESOLVER.md" → RESOLVER.md is the decision tree → each directory README.md is the local resolver → schema.md defines page structure → the enrich skill defines the enrichment protocol.**
73|
74|## Architecture
75|
76|Three layers:
77|
78|**Raw sources** — meeting transcripts, emails, tweets, web research, API responses, calendar events, contact data. Immutable. The agent reads from these but never modifies them. Stored in `sources/` and `.raw/` sidecar directories.
79|
80|**The brain** — a directory of interlinked markdown files. People pages, company pages, deal pages, meeting pages, project pages, concept pages. The agent owns this layer entirely. It creates pages, updates them when new information arrives, maintains cross-references, and keeps everything consistent. You read it; the agent writes it.
81|
82|**The schema** — a document (this one, plus `schema.md` and `RESOLVER.md`) that tells the agent how the brain is structured, what the conventions are, and what workflows to follow. This is the key configuration file — it makes your agent a disciplined knowledge maintainer rather than a generic chatbot.
83|
84|## The Database + Markdown Architecture
85|
86|The markdown wiki is the human-facing layer — the primary interface for humans and LLMs. But it's not the sole source of truth. A structured database layer provides the foundation, and the markdown is generated from it.
87|
88|### The Four Database Primitives
89|
90|**Entity registry** — canonical ID, all aliases, all external IDs (LinkedIn member ID, X user ID, email addresses, phone numbers) in one table. This is the single source of truth for "is this the same person?" When you merge two entities, it's a database operation (point both IDs at the same canonical record), not a file-merge operation with cross-reference fixups.
91|
92|**Event ledger** — every signal that touches the brain is an immutable event: meeting attended, email received, tweet published, enrichment completed, user correction applied. Events have provenance: source, timestamp, confidence, raw payload reference. The timeline section of markdown pages is generated from this ledger. You never lose events because a page rewrite went wrong.
93|
94|**Fact store** — structured claims with provenance. "Jane Doe is CTO of Acme" with `source=crustdata, confidence=high, observed_at=2026-04-07`. When two sources disagree (LinkedIn says CTO, company website says VP Engineering), the conflict is visible as two facts for the same field with different values. The compiled truth section above the line is generated from the fact store's latest-confident values. Contradictions become data, not bugs.
95|
96|**Relationship graph** — typed edges between entities. Person→Company (role: CTO, started: 2024-01), Person→Person (relationship: co-founded company together), Company→Deal (type: Series A, date: 2025-03). Enables graph queries that markdown grep can't answer: "who do I know who's invested in AI infrastructure companies?" becomes a traversal, not a prayer.
97|
98|### Why This Matters
99|
100|- **Identity resolution** becomes a database operation (merge entity IDs), not a file-merge operation with manual cross-reference fixups
101|- **Contradictions are structural** (two facts with different values for the same field and different sources) rather than textual (hoping the LLM notices a discrepancy buried in prose)
102|- **Concurrency is solved** — events append to a ledger, facts upsert to a store, markdown is rebuilt. No more merge conflicts on shared files
103|- **Graph queries work** — "who do I know at this company?" and "what companies has this investor backed that I also know the founders of?" become database queries, not impossible grep chains
104|
105|### File-Layer Conventions
106|
107|The markdown layer uses conventions that map directly to the database primitives:
108|
109|1. **Use frontmatter for structured metadata** — anything you'd want to filter on (role, company, stage, score, tags) goes in YAML frontmatter, not buried in prose. Frontmatter is metadata for filters and schema-pack rules: it is not written to the fact store, and `gbrain search` / `query` do not index scalar frontmatter values (only the page body is chunked). If a value must be findable by search, also state it in the body, for example `Stage: negotiation` (#5335).
110|2. **Use `.raw/` for provenance** — save every API response with source and timestamp. These map to provenance records in the fact store.
111|3. **Treat the timeline as an event stream** — dated, sourced, append-only. These map to the event ledger.
112|4. **Keep compiled truth conceptually separate from evidence** — above the line is synthesis; below the line is evidence. The synthesis is a generated view; the evidence is queryable records.
113|5. **Use canonical slugs consistently** — every cross-reference uses the filename slug. These are the entity IDs in the registry.
114|
115|## Directory Structure
116|
117|```
118|brain/
119|├── RESOLVER.md        — master decision tree for filing (agent reads this first)
120|├── schema.md          — page conventions, templates, workflows
121|├── index.md           — content catalog with one-line summaries
122|├── log.md             — chronological record of all ingests/updates
123|├── people/            — one page per human being
124|│   ├── README.md      — resolver: what goes here, what doesn't
125|│   └── .raw/          — raw API responses per person (JSON sidecars)
126|├── companies/         — one page per organization
127|│   ├── README.md
128|│   └── .raw/
129|├── deals/             — financial transactions with terms and decisions
130|│   └── README.md
131|├── meetings/          — records of specific events with transcripts
132|│   └── README.md
133|├── projects/          — things being actively built (has a repo, spec, or team)
134|│   └── README.md
135|├── ideas/             — raw possibilities nobody is building yet
136|│   └── README.md
137|├── concepts/          — mental models and frameworks you'd teach
138|│   └── README.md
139|├── writing/           — prose artifacts (essays, philosophy, drafts)
140|│   └── README.md
141|├── programs/          — major life workstreams (the forest, not the trees)
142|│   └── README.md
143|├── org/               — your institution's strategy and operations
144|│   └── README.md
145|├── civic/             — political landscape, policy, government
146|│   └── README.md
147|├── media/             — public narrative, content ops, social monitoring
148|│   └── README.md
149|├── personal/          — private notes, health, personal reflections
150|│   └── README.md
151|├── household/         — domestic operations, properties, logistics
152|│   └── README.md
153|├── hiring/            — candidate pipelines and evaluations
154|│   └── README.md
155|├── sources/           — raw data imports and archived snapshots
156|│   └── README.md
157|├── prompts/           — reusable LLM prompt library
158|├── inbox/             — unsorted quick captures (temporary)
159|└── archive/           — dead pages, historical record
160|```
161|
162|Every directory has a README.md resolver. Adapt directories to your life — add or remove domains as needed. Not everyone needs civic/ or hiring/ or household/. The invariant is: **one directory per knowledge domain, one file per entity, every directory has a resolver, and RESOLVER.md is the master decision tree that guarantees MECE filing.**
163|
164|## Entity Identity and Deduplication
165|
166|In a system fed by meetings, email, social media, contacts, and APIs, **entity identity is the first real failure mode.** Without a canonical identity layer, you will end up with subtle split-brain pages — "Jane Smith" from a meeting transcript and "J. Smith" from an email and "jsmith" from Twitter all creating separate pages for the same person.
167|
168|### Canonical slugs
169|
170|Every entity gets a canonical slug that serves as its stable ID:
171|- People: `first-last.md` (all lowercase, hyphens for spaces)
172|- Companies: `company-name.md`
173|- If collisions arise, disambiguate: `david-liu-crustdata.md`, `david-liu-meta.md`
174|
175|The filename IS the identity. All references, cross-links, and .raw/ sidecars use this slug.
176|
177|### Aliases
178|
179|People have many names across sources. The frontmatter `aliases` field captures all known variants:
180|
181|```yaml
182|aliases: ["Jenny Shao", "Jenny G. Shao", "JennyGShao", "jennifer.shao@company.com"]
183|```
184|
185|Aliases include: misspellings from meeting transcripts, maiden names, nicknames, email addresses, social handles, and phonetic variants. When the enrich skill encounters a new name variant for a known entity, it adds the variant to aliases — it does NOT create a new page.
186|
187|Phone numbers are not aliases. A connector-rendered person page (Google Contacts) carries them under `phones:` in E.164 form, as exact identifiers for a deliberate `entity_identity_link` join; a digit string in `aliases` would match mentions it has nothing to do with.
188|
189|### Deduplication protocol
190|
191|Before creating any new page, the agent must:
192|1. Search existing pages by name (exact and fuzzy)
193|2. Search aliases across all pages: `grep -rl "NAME_VARIANT" /data/brain/people/ --include="*.md"`
194|3. Check .raw/ sidecars for matching email addresses or social handles
195|4. If a match is found → UPDATE the existing page (add alias if the name variant is new)
196|5. If no match → CREATE a new page
197|
198|### Merge protocol
199|
200|When you discover two pages are the same person:
201|1. Pick the more complete page as the survivor
202|2. Merge all timeline entries from the duplicate into the survivor (chronological order)
203|3. Merge all aliases
204|4. Update all cross-references that pointed to the duplicate
205|5. Delete the duplicate
206|6. Commit with message: `merge: [duplicate] into [survivor]`
207|
208|During weekly lint, actively look for potential duplicates: similar names, same company, same email across different pages.
209|
210|## Key Disambiguation Rules
211|
212|The most common filing confusions and how to resolve them:
213|
214|- **Concept vs. Idea:** Could you *teach* it as a framework? → concept. Could you *build* it? → idea.
215|- **Concept vs. Personal:** Would you share it in a professional talk? → concept. Is it private reflection? → personal.
216|- **Idea vs. Project:** Is anyone working on it? Yes → project. No → idea. The graduation moment is when work starts.
217|- **Writing vs. Media:** Writing is the *artifact* (the essay). Media is the *production and distribution infrastructure* (content pipeline, social monitoring).
218|- **Writing vs. Concepts:** A concept page is distilled (200 words of compiled truth). An essay is developed prose (argument, narrative, story).
219|- **Person vs. Company:** Is it about *them as a human*? → people/. Is it about *the organization*? → companies/. Both pages link to each other.
220|- **Household vs. Personal:** Would a PA execute on it? → household (operational). Is it private reflection? → personal.
221|- **Sources vs. .raw/ sidecars:** Per-entity enrichment data → .raw/ sidecar. Bulk multi-entity imports → sources/.
222|
223|When nothing fits, file in inbox/ and flag it. That's a signal the schema needs to evolve.
224|
225|## Page Types and Templates
226|
227|### Person
228|
229|The most important page type. A great person page is a well-researched briefing — not a LinkedIn scrape.
230|
231|```markdown
232|# Person Name
233|
234|> Executive summary: who they are, why they matter, what you should
235|> know walking into any interaction with them.
236|
237|## State
238|- **Role:** Current title
239|- **Company:** Current org
240|- **Relationship:** To you (friend, colleague, investor, etc.)
241|- **Key context:** 2-4 bullets of what matters right now
242|
243|## What They Believe
244|Worldview, positions, first principles. The hills they die on.
245|Every claim must cite its source and type:
246|- [Belief] — observed: [tweet/meeting/article, date]
247|- [Belief] — self-described: [interview/bio, date]
248|- [Belief] — inferred: [pattern across N interactions, confidence: high/medium/low]
249|
250|## What They're Building
251|Current projects, recent ships, product direction.
252|
253|## What Motivates Them
254|Ambition drivers, career arc, what gets them out of bed.
255|Distinguish between what they say motivates them (self-described) and
256|what their behavior suggests (observed/inferred).
257|
258|## Communication Style
259|How they prefer to communicate. How they handle disagreement.
260|What energizes them in conversation.
261|This section is high-value but requires careful sourcing.
262|Rules: only write here from direct observation (meeting behavior,
263|language in emails/tweets, visible patterns). Never generalize
264|from a single data point. Mark confidence level.
265|
266|## Hobby Horses
267|Topics they return to obsessively. Recurring themes in their public voice.
268|
269|## Assessment
270|- **Strengths:** What they're great at. Be specific.
271|- **Gaps:** Where they could grow. Be specific and fair.
272|- **Net read:** One-line synthesis.
273|- **Confidence:** high (5+ interactions) / medium (2-4) / low (1 or inferred)
274|- **Last assessed:** YYYY-MM-DD
275|
276|## Trajectory
277|Ascending, plateauing, pivoting, declining? Evidence.
278|
279|## Relationship
280|History of interactions, temperature, dynamic.
281|
282|## Contact
283|- Email, phone, LinkedIn, X handle, location
284|
285|## Network
286|- **Close to:** People they're frequently seen with
287|- **Crew:** Which cluster they belong to
288|
289|## Open Threads
290|- Active items, pending intros, follow-ups
291|
292|---
293|
294|## Timeline
295|- **YYYY-MM-DD** | Source — What happened.
296|```
297|
298|The timeline row grammar is `- **YYYY-MM-DD** | Source — Summary`. The
299|`Source — Summary` delimiter is a dash with a space on each side: the em dash
300|(`—`), the en dash (`–`) and the plain hyphen (` - `) are all accepted, so a
301|house style that never types an em dash writes
302|`- **2026-01-03** | Meeting - Agreed on the Q2 plan` and gets `source: Meeting`.
303|A colon is not a delimiter: `- **2026-01-02** | Meeting: Agreed on the Q2 plan`
304|still parses as a dated entry, but its source is recorded as `markdown` and the
305|whole `Meeting: Agreed on the Q2 plan` text is the summary, because `Note: …`
306|and `TODO: …` are ordinary prose. gbrain's own writers (`add_timeline_entry`,
307|the extractors) keep writing the em dash.
308|
309|All sections are optional — include what you have and omit a section until there is something to put under it (`gbrain lint` flags an empty section, `[No data yet]` included). **The template itself is a prompt for future enrichment.** A section the page lacks tells the agent what to look for next time it encounters this person.
310|
311|The principle: facts are table stakes. Context is the value.
312|
313|### Epistemic discipline on people pages
314|
315|The context sections (Beliefs, Motivations, Communication Style, Assessment) are the highest-value parts of the system but also the most prone to hallucination. An agent can over-generalize from sparse evidence or overfit to one recent interaction. Rules:
316|
317|- **Every claim cites its source.** Not "she's aggressive" but "she pushed back hard on pricing in the March 15 meeting (observed)."
318|- **Three source types:** `observed` (you saw it happen), `self-described` (they said it about themselves), `inferred` (you're reading between lines). Label each.
319|- **Confidence tracks interaction count.** One meeting = low confidence. Five meetings = high. Don't write definitive assessments from thin data.
320|- **Recency matters.** A belief from 2 years ago may not be current. Mark dates.
321|- **Never generalize from a single data point.** "She seemed frustrated in one meeting" is a timeline entry. Patterns require multiple observations.
322|- **The user's corrections override everything.** If the user says "that's wrong about her," update immediately — that correction is the highest-confidence signal in the system.
323|
324|### Company

333|- **Stage:** Seed / Series A / Growth / Public

335|- **Key metrics:** Revenue, headcount, funding

364|### Deal, Project, Concept — same pattern. Compiled truth on top, timeline on bottom.
365|
366|## The Enrichment Pipeline
367|
368|**This is the most important operational pattern.** Every time your agent encounters a person or company — in a meeting, email, tweet, calendar event, contact sync — it should enrich the corresponding brain page.
369|
370|Enrichment is not just "look up their LinkedIn." It's:
371|
372|- **What they believe** — positions, worldview, public stances
373|- **What they're building** — current projects, what's shipping
374|- **What motivates them** — ambition, career trajectory
375|- **Their communication style** — how they engage, what energizes them
376|- **Their relationship to you** — history, context, open threads
377|- **Hard facts** — role, company, contact info, funding (table stakes)
378|
379|Facts are table stakes. Context is the value.
380|
381|### When to enrich
382|
383|**Any time** a person or company signal appears:
384|- Someone is mentioned in a meeting transcript → enrich
385|- Someone emails you → enrich
386|- Someone interacts with you on social media → enrich
387|- A new contact appears → enrich
388|- You mention someone in conversation and their page is thin → enrich
389|- A company announces funding, ships a product, makes news → enrich
390|
391|### Enrichment sources (in order of value)
392|
393|1. **Your own interactions** — what you said about them, what they said to you (highest signal)
394|2. **Meeting transcripts** — richest context source
395|3. **Email threads** — tone, urgency, relationship dynamics
396|4. **Social media** — beliefs, public positioning, who they engage with
397|5. **Web search** — background, press, talks
398|6. **People APIs** — structured profile data (career history, education, skills, contact info)
399|7. **Company APIs** — funding, investors, valuations, headcount, financials
400|8. **Contact data** — email, phone, location
401|
402|### Data source skills
403|
404|Each external data source should be its own named skill with full API documentation, auth patterns, and usage notes. The enrich skill orchestrates them — it decides *which* sources to call based on tier, then delegates to the individual skill for *how* to call the API.
405|
406|This keeps things DRY: the enrich skill owns the logic (when to enrich, what tier, what to extract), and each data source skill owns the API contract (endpoints, auth, rate limits, gotchas, validation rules).
407|
408|Recommended data source skills:
409|
410|- **Web search** — broad keyword search (Brave, Google, etc.). Quick background, press, funding.
411|- **Semantic search** — better than keyword for finding specific people, LinkedIn URLs, personal writing. (Exa, Perplexity, etc.)
412|- **Social search** — X/Twitter, Bluesky, etc. for public voice: beliefs, projects, engagement patterns.
413|- **People enrichment** — structured LinkedIn-like data: career history, education, skills, contact info. (Crustdata, Proxycurl, People Data Labs, etc.)
414|- **Network search** — search your professional network for warm intros and connections. (Happenstance, Clay, etc.)
415|- **Company intelligence** — Pitchbook-grade data: funding rounds, investors, valuations, headcount, financials. (Captain API, Crunchbase, etc.)
416|- **Meeting history** — search past meetings for interactions with this entity. (Circleback, Otter, Fireflies, etc.)
417|- **Contact data** — email, phone, location from your contacts. (Google Contacts, etc.)
418|
419|The typical enrichment flow for a new person:
420|1. **Network search** → find LinkedIn URL, career arc, alternate names
421|2. **People enrichment** → deep structured data (skills, work history, education, contact info)
422|3. **Semantic search** → find personal sites, talks, writing that reveal beliefs and perspective
423|4. **Social search** → their public voice, who they engage with, hobby horses
424|5. **Web search** → press coverage, recent news, talks
425|6. **Meeting history** → past interactions with you
426|
427|For a new company:
428|1. **Company intelligence** → funding, investors, headcount, financials
429|2. **Web search** → product, press, traction
430|3. **Social search** → company's public positioning
431|4. **People enrichment** → enrich founders/key team members (each triggers person enrichment)
432|
433|### Enrichment tiers (don't over-enrich)
434|
435|- **Tier 1 (key people):** Full pipeline — all sources. Inner circle, business partners, important collaborators.
436|- **Tier 2 (notable):** Web search + social + brain cross-reference. People you interact with occasionally.
437|- **Tier 3 (minor mentions):** Extract signal from source only, append to timeline. Everyone else worth tracking.
438|
439|A thin page with real interaction data is better than a fat page stuffed with generic web results. Don't waste 10 API calls on someone with no public presence.
440|
441|### Raw data sidecars
442|
443|Every enrichment API response gets saved as a JSON sidecar:
444|
445|```
446|people/jane-doe.md              ← brain page (curated, readable)
447|people/.raw/jane-doe.json       ← raw API responses
448|```
449|
450|The JSON is keyed by source with fetch timestamps:
451|
452|```json
453|{
454|  "sources": {
455|    "crustdata": { "fetched_at": "2026-04-05T...", "data": { ... } },
456|    "web_search": { "fetched_at": "...", "data": { ... } }
457|  }
458|}
459|```
460|
461|The brain page is the distilled version. Raw data is the archive.
462|
463|What goes in the brain page (distilled): location, current title, company, headline, education (one line), career arc (condensed), top skills, social handles, profile picture permalink.
464|
465|What stays in .raw/ only: full work history with job descriptions, complete skill lists, company descriptions for each employer, platform-specific IDs, follower/connection counts, full API response bodies.
466|
467|When re-enriching: overwrite the source key with fresh data + new timestamp. Don't append — replace.
468|
469|### Validation rules
470|
471|When auto-enriching from people/company APIs:
472|- **Low connection/follower count (e.g., <20):** Likely wrong person. Save to .raw/ with a `"validation": "low_connections"` flag. Don't auto-write to the brain page.
473|- **Name mismatch:** If the returned name doesn't share a last name with the entity, skip.
474|- **Obviously joke profiles:** Career arcs mentioning absurd titles — skip.
475|- **When in doubt:** Save raw data but don't update the brain page. Wrong data is worse than no data.
476|
477|### Browser budget
478|
479|If enrichment involves browser-based lookups (LinkedIn, authenticated pages), set a daily budget (e.g., 20 lookups/day) to avoid account flagging. Prefer API-based enrichment services for bulk work — they don't touch the user's browser session.
480|
481|## Entry Criteria — Who Gets a Page
482|
483|Not everyone deserves a brain page. Scale page creation to relationship importance:
484|
485|**Always create a page for:**
486|- Anyone you've had a 1:1 or small-group meeting with
487|- Key colleagues, partners, and direct collaborators
488|- Anyone with a strong working relationship or better
489|- Family, close friends, inner circle
490|
491|**Create if signal exists:**
492|- People from contacts with recent interaction
493|- Anyone mentioned by name in conversation with context
494|- Event contacts with multiple shared events
495|
496|**Do NOT create:**
497|- Random names from mass event guest lists with no interaction
498|- Single-name entries with no identifying context
499|- Contacts with no relationship signal at all
500|
501|When in doubt: does the user benefit from this entry existing? If no, skip it.
502|
503|## The Skill Architecture
504|
505|Skills are the modular building blocks of the system. There are three types, and understanding how they compose is critical.
506|
507|### 1. Data source skills (leaf nodes)
508|
509|Each external API or data source gets its own named skill. The skill owns the API contract: endpoints, authentication, rate limits, error handling, validation rules, and what the response looks like.
510|
511|Examples:
512|- **People enrichment** (Crustdata, Proxycurl, People Data Labs) — structured LinkedIn-like data
513|- **Network search** (Happenstance, Clay) — search professional network, find mutual connections
514|- **Company intelligence** (Captain API/Pitchbook, Crunchbase) — funding, investors, financials
515|- **Semantic search** (Exa, Perplexity) — find LinkedIn URLs, personal sites, writing
516|- **Meeting history** (Circleback, Otter, Fireflies) — past meeting transcripts and notes
517|- **Calendar/contacts** (Google Calendar, Google Contacts via integration tools) — schedule, contact info
518|- **Social media** (X API, Bluesky API) — public posts, engagement, follower data
519|- **Workspace tools** (Gmail, Slack, Drive via integration tools) — email threads, messages, documents
520|
521|Data source skills are **never called directly by the user.** They're called by orchestration skills (below).
522|
523|### 2. Orchestration skills (coordinators)
524|
525|These skills contain the *logic* — they decide what to do, then delegate to data source skills for how to do it.
526|
527|**The enrich skill** is the most important orchestration skill. It decides:
528|- Is this a CREATE (new page) or UPDATE (new signal)?
529|- What tier is this entity? (determines which data sources to call)
530|- What signal types to extract from the source material?
531|- Which data source skills to call, in what order?
532|- How to write the results to the brain?
533|
534|Other orchestration skills:
535|- **Meeting ingestion** — pulls meetings from a meeting tool, creates brain meeting pages with analysis, then calls enrich for every attendee and company discussed
536|- **Email triage / executive assistant** — processes inbox, handles scheduling, then calls enrich when it encounters people or companies
537|- **Social monitoring** — scans public social media for mentions and engagement, then calls enrich for notable accounts
538|
539|### 3. Pipeline skills (end-to-end workflows)
540|
541|These are the user-facing skills that chain multiple orchestration and data source skills together:
542|- **Morning briefing** — reads calendar + tasks + brain state + recent signals → produces a briefing
543|- **Person research** — given a name, runs full Tier 1 enrichment and presents the result
544|- **Weekly brain maintenance** — runs lint, flags stale pages, suggests enrichment targets
545|
546|### How they compose
547|
548|```
549|User says "tell me about Jane Doe"
550|  → Agent searches brain (grep/index)
551|  → Page is thin → calls enrich skill (orchestration)
552|    → enrich determines Tier 1
553|    → calls happenstance skill (data source) → gets LinkedIn URL
554|    → calls crustdata skill (data source) → gets full profile
555|    → calls exa skill (data source) → finds personal writing
556|    → calls web_search (built-in tool) → gets press coverage
557|    → calls meeting history (data source) → finds past meetings
558|    → writes brain page, saves .raw/ sidecar, cross-references
559|  → Agent presents the enriched page to user
560|```
561|
562|```
563|Cron fires "meeting ingestion" every afternoon
564|  → meeting-ingestion skill (orchestration) pulls new meetings
565|  → for each meeting: creates brain meeting page
566|  → for each attendee: calls enrich skill (orchestration)
567|    → enrich calls relevant data source skills based on tier
568|  → for each company discussed: calls enrich skill
569|  → extracts tasks, commits brain repo
570|```
571|
572|The key insight: **data source skills are stateless and reusable.** The enrich skill can call Crustdata whether the trigger was a meeting, an email, a social mention, or a direct user request. The data source skill doesn't care where the request came from.
573|
574|## How Enrich Wires Into Everything
575|
576|The enrich skill is the central hub. Every ingest pathway converges on it:
577|
578|```
579|Meeting ingestion ───────┬─────────────────────────┬─── people enrichment API
580|Email triage ────────────┤                         ├─── company intelligence API
581|Social monitoring ───────┤    ENRICH SKILL         ├─── network search API
582|Contact sync ────────────┤   (orchestration)       ├─── semantic search API
583|Manual conversation ─────┤                         ├─── social search API
584|Calendar events ─────────┤                         ├─── web search
585|Webhooks ────────────────┴─────────────────────────┴─── meeting history API
586|                              │
587|                              ▼
588|                         BRAIN REPO
589|                    (people/, companies/,
590|                     meetings/, deals/)
591|```
592|
593|Every arrow into the enrich skill carries a **signal** (the raw information from the source) and an **entity** (the person or company to enrich). The enrich skill:
594|
595|1. **Checks brain state** — does a page exist? Is it thin?
596|2. **Determines tier** — Tier 1 (full pipeline), Tier 2 (web + social + cross-ref), Tier 3 (source extraction only)
597|3. **Extracts signal** from the source material (beliefs, motivations, trajectory, facts)
598|4. **Calls data source skills** based on tier (each skill is a named, documented module)
599|5. **Writes to brain** — CREATE (via RESOLVER.md) or UPDATE (append timeline, update compiled truth)
600|6. **Cross-references** — updates all linked entity pages
601|7. **Saves raw data** to `.raw/` sidecar
602|8. **Commits** to the brain repo
603|
604|The critical wiring rule: **every ingest skill must call enrich.** This is not optional or aspirational. It's structural. If a new ingest pathway is added (say, a Slack monitoring skill), its implementation must include "for each person/company mentioned, call the enrich skill." If that line is missing, the brain stops compounding from that source.
605|
606|## Automated Cron Jobs
607|
608|The brain doesn't just grow when you're actively using it. Cron jobs make the system autonomous — the brain is maintained, the inbox is triaged, meetings are ingested, and mentions are monitored even while you sleep.
609|
610|### The cron architecture
611|
612|Cron jobs run as **isolated agent sessions** — they get their own context, read their own skills, and don't block the main conversation thread. They can post to specific notification channels (Telegram topics, Slack channels, Discord threads) or work silently.
613|
614|Each cron job is essentially: "wake up, read a skill, do the work, post results (or stay silent if nothing happened), go back to sleep."
615|
616|### Recommended cron jobs for a brain-powered system
617|
618|**High frequency (every 10-30 minutes):**
619|- **Email monitor** — scan inbox, classify by priority, post digest to a notification channel. Handle low-risk items (scheduling, acknowledgments) directly.
620|- **Message monitor** — check key communication channels for unreplied messages from important contacts. Surface them with suggested responses.
621|
622|**Medium frequency (every 1-3 hours):**
623|- **Social radar** — scan public social media for mentions of you or your organization, engagement, emerging narratives. Alert on items that need attention. Call enrich for notable new accounts engaging with you.
624|- **Heartbeat** — the omnibus check. Calendar lookahead, task review, email scan, brain state review. Post if something needs attention; stay silent if not.
625|
626|**Daily:**
627|- **Morning briefing** — calendar + tasks + urgent items + overnight signals → one notification. The "here's your day" message.
628|- **Task prep** — archive yesterday's completed tasks, build today's list from calendar + backlog + recurring items.
629|- **Meeting ingestion** — pull all new meetings from your meeting tool, run full ingestion (create meeting pages, propagate to entity pages, extract tasks). This is the heaviest cron job — it touches the most brain pages.
630|- **Social media collection** — archive your own posts, track engagement velocity, detect deletions. Feed into media/ pages.
631|
632|**Weekly:**
633|- **Brain lint** — run the full maintenance pass: contradictions, stale pages, orphans, missing cross-references, MECE filing violations. Post a report.
634|- **Enrichment sweep** — find brain pages that haven't been enriched in 90+ days, or pages missing many of their type's template sections. Queue them for re-enrichment.
635|- **Contact sync** — pull recent additions from your contacts, cross-reference with brain. Create pages for significant new contacts.
636|
637|### How crons feed the brain
638|
639|The key insight: **cron jobs are the autonomous enrichment engine.** Without them, the brain only grows when you're actively talking to the agent. With them:
640|
641|- The email monitor encounters a person → calls enrich → brain grows
642|- The meeting ingestion processes a transcript → calls enrich for every attendee → brain grows
643|- The social radar detects a new notable account → calls enrich → brain grows
644|- The contact sync finds a new contact → calls enrich → brain grows
645|- The enrichment sweep finds stale pages → calls enrich with fresh data → brain stays current
646|
647|The brain compounds 24/7 because the cron jobs are wired to call enrich. The user sleeps; the brain doesn't.
648|
649|### Cron job design rules
650|
651|1. **Silent when nothing happens.** If a cron finds nothing new, it should produce no output. No "nothing to report" messages. This is critical — noisy crons get disabled.
652|2. **Post to specific channels.** Each cron posts to its designated notification channel (e.g., email cron → Emails topic, social radar → Social Alerts topic). Don't mix signals.
653|3. **Spawn sub-agents for heavy work.** The cron session should stay lightweight. If meeting ingestion needs to process 5 meetings and update 30 entity pages, spawn sub-agents for the entity propagation.
654|4. **Idempotent and checkpoint-aware.** Every cron should track what it's already processed (in a state file like `meeting-notes-state.json`) so it doesn't redo work on the next run.
655|5. **Respect quiet hours.** Don't post between 11 PM and 7 AM unless something is genuinely urgent. Crons should check the time before posting.
656|6. **Every ingest cron must call enrich.** This is the structural rule. A cron that processes meetings but doesn't enrich attendees is a bug, not a feature.
657|
658|### Example: how it all fits together
659|
660|A typical afternoon in an autonomous brain system:
661|
662|1. **3:00 PM** — Email monitor cron fires. Scans inbox. Finds 3 new emails: a scheduling request, a funding announcement, and a founder asking for advice.
663|   - Handles the scheduling request directly (checks calendar, replies with available times)
664|   - Calls enrich on the company in the funding announcement → updates company page with new round
665|   - Posts the founder's email to notification channel for the user to handle
666|
667|2. **3:15 PM** — Meeting ingestion cron fires. Finds 2 new meetings from today.
668|   - Creates 2 brain meeting pages with analysis
669|   - Calls enrich for 8 attendees across both meetings → updates 8 people pages
670|   - Calls enrich for 3 companies discussed → updates 3 company pages
671|   - Extracts 4 action items → adds to task list
672|
673|3. **3:30 PM** — Social radar cron fires. Detects a journalist writing a thread about the user's organization.
674|   - Posts alert to Social Alerts channel
675|   - Calls enrich on the journalist → creates/updates their people page with recent activity
676|
677|4. **4:00 PM** — Heartbeat fires. Calendar shows a meeting in 1 hour. Brain page for the attendee was last enriched 3 months ago.
678|   - Triggers a fresh enrichment pass on the attendee
679|   - Posts a prep note: "Meeting with X in 1 hour. Here's what's changed since you last met."
680|
681|The user didn't ask for any of this. The brain grew by 12 pages and the user walked into their 4:00 PM meeting fully prepared — because the plumbing is wired correctly.

687|### Example 1: Meeting Ingestion — The Full Chain
688|
689|A cron job fires at 3:00 PM daily with the prompt: "Read skills/meeting-ingestion/SKILL.md and process today's meetings."
690|
691|**Step 1: Skill chain loads.** The meeting-ingestion skill's preamble says "Read skills/enrich/SKILL.md" — so the agent loads the enrichment protocol before touching any data. This is critical: it means the agent knows how to handle every person and company it encounters.
692|
693|**Step 2: Pull new meetings.** The agent calls the meeting history data source skill (in this system, Circleback). It checks a state file (`memory/meeting-notes-state.json`) that tracks the last processed meeting ID. Finds 2 new meetings since last run.
694|
695|**Step 3: Process Meeting 1 — "Product Review with Sarah Chen and Mike Torres."**
696|
697|The agent creates `brain/meetings/2026-04-07-product-review.md` with:
698|- Its own analysis above the line (not a copy of the AI summary — reframed through what the brain already knows about the attendees and the project)
699|- Key decisions, action items, and connections to other brain pages
700|- Full transcript below the line
701|
702|**Step 4: Enrich attendees.**
703|
704|For **Sarah Chen** — the agent searches the brain: `grep -rl "Sarah Chen" /data/brain/people/`. Finds `people/sarah-chen.md`. Reads it. Page was last enriched 2 weeks ago and has good coverage. → **Tier 3**: extract signal from this meeting only. Appends to her timeline: "2026-04-07 | Meeting — Pushed back on timeline for launch, wants more QA. Concerned about API stability." Updates her Open Threads with the new follow-up item.
705|
706|For **Mike Torres** — brain search finds `people/mike-torres.md`. Page exists but is thin: just a name, title, and one previous meeting entry. → **Tier 2**: web search + social + brain cross-reference. Agent finds his recent blog posts (feeds into What They Believe), his X activity (feeds into Hobby Horses), and cross-references him with two other brain pages that mention him. Updates compiled truth above the line.

708|For **"Alex from Meridian Labs"** (mentioned in the meeting but not an attendee) — brain search finds nothing. → **CREATE path**:
709|1. Reads RESOLVER.md: "a specific named person" → `people/`
710|2. Creates `people/alex-rivera.md` using the person template from schema.md
711|3. Runs **Tier 1 enrichment** (full pipeline): network search → finds LinkedIn URL. People enrichment API → full structured profile. Semantic search → finds a conference talk. Web search → finds press coverage of Meridian Labs' recent funding.
712|4. Saves raw API responses to `people/.raw/alex-rivera.json`
713|5. Cross-references: updates `companies/meridian-labs.md` to link to Alex's page

715|**Step 5: Enrich companies discussed.** Meridian Labs was discussed extensively. Agent checks `companies/meridian-labs.md` — exists but funding data is 4 months stale. Calls company intelligence API → gets fresh round data. Updates the page.

719|**Step 7: Repeat for Meeting 2.** Same flow.

871|## Ingest Workflows
872|
873|These are the specific ingest patterns. Each one calls enrich as its terminal step.
874|
875|### Meeting ingestion
876|
877|After every meeting (via Circleback, Otter, Fireflies, or manual notes):
878|
879|1. Pull meeting notes + full transcript
880|2. Create a brain meeting page with **your own analysis** (not just regurgitated AI summary) — reframe through what you know about the attendees' world
881|3. **Propagate to entity pages** — call enrich for every person and company discussed. A meeting is NOT fully ingested until entity pages are updated.
882|4. Extract action items to task list
883|5. Commit
884|
885|### Email ingestion
886|
887|When processing email:
888|- Extract people and companies mentioned
889|- Call enrich with email context (tone, requests, relationship signals)
890|- Note scheduling, commitments, follow-ups
891|

893|
894|When monitoring social media:
895|- Capture what people you track are saying publicly (beliefs, projects, opinions)
896|- Detect engagement patterns (who's replying to you, who's amplifying you)
897|- Call enrich for notable accounts → feed into "What They Believe" and "Hobby Horses" sections

900|
901|When you mention someone or something in conversation:
902|- Your own comments are the highest-value signal — always capture these
903|- "Really sharp on the technical side, could be a good advisor for the infra project" → that goes in the person's page immediately
904|- If the brain page is thin, trigger a full enrichment
